title: What counts as an emergency situation under federal law
rule_summary: Under 21 CFR 290.10, for the purpose of authorizing an ORAL prescription of a Schedule II controlled substance, an EMERGENCY SITUATION means those situations in which the prescribing practitioner determines: (a) that IMMEDIATE ADMINISTRATION of the controlled substance is necessary for proper treatment of the intended ultimate user; AND (b) that NO APPROPRIATE ALTERNATIVE TREATMENT IS AVAILABLE, including administration of a drug which is not a Schedule II controlled substance; AND (c) that it is NOT REASONABLY POSSIBLE for the prescribing practitioner to provide a WRITTEN prescription to be presented to the person dispensing the substance prior to the dispensing. All three elements are the prescribing practitioner's determination.
exam_relevance: Tests the gate that must be satisfied before the emergency oral pathway opens at all, and in particular the no-alternative-treatment element that the Massachusetts definition does not carry.
exceptions: The three elements are conjunctive; failing any one means the situation is not an emergency situation for this purpose.
common_confusions: Omitting the no-appropriate-alternative-treatment element, which federal law requires and Massachusetts does not state.
Reading element (c) as impossibility of an ELECTRONIC prescription; the federal element is keyed to a WRITTEN prescription.
Treating the determination as the pharmacist's; all three elements are determined by the prescribing practitioner.
verification_notes: 21 CFR 290.10 read verbatim in the current eCFR text on 2026-09-10.
